p: In the year twelve hundred and six, at a great assembly of the tribes beside the river Onon, in the grasslands of what is now Mongolia, a chieftain named Temujin was proclaimed ruler of all the peoples who lived in felt tents, and took the title Chinggis Khan, which we write Genghis Khan, and which seems to mean something like universal or oceanic ruler. He was then perhaps forty years old. He had been born into a minor noble family, abandoned with his mother and brothers after his father was poisoned, reduced to living on roots and fish, enslaved for a time by a rival clan, and had risen, by ferocity, cunning, and an extraordinary gift for binding men to him, to unite the quarrelsome tribes of the steppe for the first time in their history. Within seventy years, his sons and grandsons ruled the largest continuous land empire the world has ever seen, from Korea to Hungary, from Siberia to the Persian Gulf. Only the British Empire of the century to come, the Encyclopaedia informs me, has ever covered more of the globe, and that was scattered across the oceans.

The Mongols were herdsmen and horsemen. Every man was a soldier, trained from childhood to ride and to shoot with a powerful bow of horn and sinew from the saddle at full gallop. Each warrior led several spare horses, so that a Mongol army could move at speeds that astonished its enemies, sometimes covering sixty miles in a day. Chinggis organised his army in units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand, deliberately mixing men of different tribes, so that their loyalty was to him and not to their clans, and promoted his officers for ability rather than birth. The army practised feigned retreats, luring the enemy into pursuit and then turning on them. It employed spies and scouts to an extent unknown in Europe. And it learned quickly: taking Chinese and Persian engineers into its service, it acquired the art of siege warfare, which no army of horsemen had possessed before.

The Mongols also employed terror as a deliberate method. A city that surrendered at once was usually spared, though heavily taxed. A city that resisted was often destroyed, and its inhabitants, apart from craftsmen and others who might be useful, slaughtered. The chroniclers give figures for the dead in the cities of Persia, at Merv, at Nishapur, at Herat, of hundreds of thousands or more. These figures are surely exaggerated, but the destruction was real, and some regions of Persia and Central Asia took centuries to recover. The ancient irrigation works of the region, once destroyed, were in places never rebuilt.

Chinggis conquered the kingdoms of northern China and the empire of Khwarezm in Central Asia and Persia, whose ruler had unwisely murdered his envoys. He died in twelve twenty-seven, and was buried in a secret place, which, the Encyclopaedia says, has never been found. His son Ogedei continued the conquests. In twelve forty-one, Mongol armies destroyed the armies of Poland and Hungary within days of each other, and Western Europe lay open before them. Then news arrived of Ogedei's death, and the princes went home to choose a successor. Europe was spared, not by its knights, but by the Mongol law of succession. In twelve fifty-eight, as I have said, they took Baghdad and ended the caliphate of the Abbasids. They were stopped in Syria in twelve sixty, at a place called Ain Jalut, the Spring of Goliath, by the Mamluks of Egypt, a remarkable military caste of slave-soldiers, many of them of the same steppe stock as the Mongols themselves. Kublai Khan, grandson of Chinggis, completed the conquest of southern China in twelve seventy-nine and founded the Yuan dynasty, with his capital at what is now Peking. His two attempts to invade Japan were destroyed by storms, which the Japanese called kamikaze, the divine wind, a word that the twentieth century will turn to darker use.

Once the conquests were over, the Mongol rulers proved, on the whole, tolerant and practical. They allowed all religions, and Buddhists, Muslims, Christians and Taoists debated before the khans. They protected merchants, and established a system of relay stations across the empire, at which messengers could change horses and riders, so that news travelled across Asia with astonishing speed. Under what historians call the Pax Mongolica, from the Latin for the Mongol peace, the trade routes of Asia were safer than ever before or for centuries after. Marco Polo of Venice spent some seventeen years in Kublai Khan's service and wrote of his travels a book that set Europe dreaming of the riches of Cathay. Christopher Columbus took a copy of it with him across the Atlantic, with notes in his own hand in the margins.

The empire was too large to hold together. Within two generations it split into four great khanates: the Yuan in China; the Ilkhanate in Persia; the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia; and the Golden Horde on the steppes of Russia, whose khans held the Russian princes as tributaries for two hundred years, which, Russian historians maintain, profoundly shaped the character of the Russian state. The rulers in the west became Muslims; Kublai's line in China became Chinese in manner, and was driven out in thirteen sixty-eight by the Ming. The Mongol peace had also carried, along its swift roads, the plague that would kill a third of Europe, of which I speak next.

What, then, are we to make of them? The men of the future are inclined to emphasise the trade, the tolerance and the connection of East and West. My own century has emphasised the pyramids of skulls. Both are true. I would say only that the Mongols showed, for the first time, that the whole of Eurasia could be bound into a single system, and that the binding was done in blood. Whether the world was better for it, I leave to those who did not live in Nishapur.
